messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 43
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Pharmacist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 71

**Patient Vignette: "Nadia"**

Nadia is a 43-year-old married Middle Eastern woman who works as a pharmacist at a community clinic. She presents for therapy at the urging of her husband, who has grown concerned about her increasing withdrawal and irritability over the past year. She is soft-spoken, meticulously dressed, and sits with her hands folded tightly in her lap. She apologizes twice for "wasting my time" before beginning her story.

The trauma she carries is not a single event but a texture woven into her childhood. She describes her mother as a woman of immense intelligence and even greater cruelty. Nadia was the eldest daughter in a traditional household, and from the age of seven until she left for college at eighteen, her mother would beat her with a wooden spoon, a belt, or whatever was at hand. The abuse was never about anger, Nadia explains; it was about discipline. Her mother would say, "I am teaching you to be perfect, because the world will not forgive you for being a woman who is less than perfect." The beatings were ritualized: she was made to kneel on the kitchen floor, count the blows aloud, and then thank her mother for the lesson.

Nadia left home at eighteen, married a kind, quiet man at twenty-two, and built a life of order and control. She became a pharmacist, a profession she chose for its precision. In her clinic, she is known for her encyclopedic knowledge of drug interactions and her refusal to make errors. She double-checks every prescription, sometimes three times. She keeps her workspace immaculate. At home, she organizes the pantry by expiration date and alphabetically. She has never spoken of the beatings to anyone, not even her husband. She tells herself it is in the past.

But the past is not past. Over the last year, something has shifted. It began when a new pharmacy technician, a young woman with a loud voice and a brusque manner, started working alongside her. The woman is not unkind, but she is impatient. When she snaps, "Nadia, where are the beta-blockers?" Nadia's body responds before her mind can catch up. Her heart pounds. Her palms sweat. She feels a hot flush of shame, as if she has done something wrong. She finds herself apologizing for things that are not her fault.

At home, she has become hypervigilant. She cannot bear the sound of her husband clearing his throat. It reminds her of the sound her mother made before the beatings began. She sleeps in a separate room now, claiming she has trouble with her back. In truth, she cannot tolerate the vulnerability of being asleep next to another person. She has nightmares, though she refuses to describe them. She wakes up with her fists clenched, her jaw aching from grinding her teeth.

She avoids the kitchen. When she must prepare a meal, she feels a wave of nausea. The sight of a wooden spoon in the drawer makes her freeze. She has started using only silicone utensils, though she tells her husband it is because they are "more hygienic."

Her PCL-5 score of 71 reflects the severity of her symptoms. She endorses intrusive memories nearly every day, though she has learned to push them down so quickly that she barely registers them as thoughts—only as a sudden, inexplicable surge of dread. She avoids thinking about her childhood, but avoidance has become a full-time job. She has stopped visiting her mother, excusing herself with work. She has stopped visiting her sister, because her sister's house has the same smell—cumin and rosewater—that triggers a dissociative fog.

She is not depressed, she insists. She is functional. She fills prescriptions, pays bills, attends her son's parent-teacher conferences. But she has not laughed in months. She has not cried in years. She feels like a machine that is running perfectly but has forgotten what it was built to feel.

In session, she sits very still, as if any movement might break the careful architecture of her composure. She says, "I don't understand why this is happening now. I survived it. I left. I made a good life. Why is it coming back?" She looks at me with genuine bewilderment, as if her own mind has betrayed her. She does not yet know that survival is not the same as healing. She is still kneeling on that kitchen floor, counting.
